strategy:
1. Approach and rationale
Use a feasible, projected first-order search over the sample values. At each step, minimize a smooth log-sum-exp approximation to the maximum of all finite-support correlation lags; gradually reduce its smoothing temperature so the search increasingly focuses on the true maximum. After every proposed step, project jointly onto the box and fixed-sum constraints. Run the same continuation from a deterministic portfolio of feasible starts, and select candidates only by the exact evaluator score.

This is materially different from an epigraph formulation solved by SLSQP: there is no epigraph variable and no general nonlinear constrained optimizer. The search uses a custom gradient of the smoothed maximum and an explicit capped-simplex projection; feasible points are maintained throughout. This addresses the nonsmooth maximum without discarding any lag, while allowing all N samples to move. Multiple seeded starts and continuation are heuristics that may find better local basins than a single local solve. The facts guaranteed by the design are joint feasibility of repaired candidates and exact scoring of the returned candidate, not an improvement over the parent. The products in the correlations make the problem nonconvex, so the method has no global-optimality guarantee and may stall at a local minimum.

2. Mathematical specification
Let N be the runtime sample count, h ∈ R^N, Δ = 2/N, and m = N/2. The feasible set is 0 ≤ h_i ≤ 1 for every i and Σ_i h_i = m. For every integer lag k from −(N−1) to N−1, define
q_k(h) = Σ_{i=max(0,−k)}^{min(N−1,N−1−k)} h_{i+k}(1−h_i).
The sum is over only valid indices: there is no wraparound. With NumPy’s full linear-correlation convention, q_k is the entry at index k+N−1 of np.correlate(h, 1−h, mode='full'). Thus the authoritative score is F(h) = Δ max_k q_k(h). This includes both lag directions and all partial-overlap boundary lags. Do not replace it with a circular correlation or an autocorrelation expression that omits boundary terms.

For a component r, the exact lag derivative is
∂q_k/∂h_r = 1_{0≤r−k<N}(1−h_{r−k}) − 1_{0≤r+k<N}h_{r+k}.
At k=0 the two terms combine to 1−2h_r. The q_k are quadratic or bilinear, so F is generally nonconvex and nonsmooth.

For smoothing temperature τ>0, use the upper approximation
φ_τ(h) = τ log Σ_k exp(r_k/τ), where r_k = Δq_k(h).
If rmax = max_k r_k, evaluate it stably as rmax + τ log Σ_k exp((r_k−rmax)/τ). It satisfies F(h) ≤ φ_τ(h) ≤ F(h)+τ log(2N−1). Define p_k = exp((r_k−rmax)/τ) / Σ_j exp((r_j−rmax)/τ). Its gradient is ∇φ_τ = Δ Σ_k p_k ∇q_k. This is a search surrogate only; acceptance and the returned score use F, not φ_τ.

For joint feasibility restoration, project z onto the capped simplex by minimizing ½||h−z||² subject to the box and sum constraints. The KKT conditions give h_i = clip(z_i−θ,0,1), where θ is chosen so Σ_i clip(z_i−θ,0,1) = m. This sum is monotone nonincreasing in θ, so bisection followed by a small residual correction gives a concrete joint repair. Clipping followed by separate rescaling is not a valid substitute.

3. Implementation procedure
3.1. Write one top-level run(seed=42, **kwargs) and any needed helper functions at module top level. Do not use closures or lambdas. Use NumPy float64 arrays and a seeded NumPy random generator; no external optimizer is required. Read initial_h_values from the pre-imported global when present, without redefining it or embedding, serializing, or manually reproducing its entries. Treat the supplied array as read-only. Do not depend on an unspecified signature for evaluate_erdos_solution; implement the exact score locally.

3.2. Resolve N before constructing candidates. If initial_h_values is a nonempty one-dimensional array, use its length as N and preserve that resolution; it takes precedence over kwargs. If the shape is valid but conversion or values are unusable, retain that length and use the uniform fallback. If no usable parent dimension exists, accept kwargs['n_points'] only when it is an integer-valued scalar in [1,999]; otherwise use N=70. Do not resize or interpolate a valid parent. For a parent with N>999, still preserve its dimension, but use the reduced search budget in section 4. Convert seed to an integer when possible and otherwise use 42.

3.3. Implement a top-level project_box_sum(z, N). Require a one-dimensional vector of length N with finite entries; for malformed, non-finite, or extreme-magnitude proposals, return the uniform vector of 0.5 values. Set m=N/2. For ordinary finite proposals, bracket θ by min(z)−1 and max(z), then perform 80 bisection steps. At a midpoint θ, form clip(z−θ,0,1): if its sum exceeds m, move the lower bracket up to θ; otherwise move the upper bracket down to θ. Form the clipped vector at the final midpoint. Compute residual e=m−sum(h) and distribute positive residual, in index order, into available capacities 1−h_i; distribute negative residual by subtracting from h_i in index order. Repeat a correction pass if needed. The adjustment at each coordinate must be bounded by its available room; do not independently clip and rescale afterward. If the result is non-finite, outside [0,1], or has sum error above 1e−10·max(1,N), return the uniform vector. This projection must repair every perturbed start and every proposed gradient step.

3.4. Implement a top-level lag_values(h) returning q in increasing k order, with length M=2N−1. Loop over k=−(N−1),…,N−1. For k≥0, set L=N−k, a=h[k:k+L], and b=h[0:L]; set q[k+N−1]=sum(a*(1−b)). For k<0, set d=−k, L=N−d, a=h[0:L], and b=h[d:d+L]; set q[k+N−1]=sum(a*(1−b)). These slices evaluate precisely the valid-index formula in section 2.

3.5. Implement smooth_value_grad(h, τ, N) without constructing an M-by-N Jacobian. First compute q=lag_values(h), r=(2/N)q, rmax=max(r), and stable weights p using the log-sum-exp formula. Return φ=rmax+τ log(sum(exp((r−rmax)/τ))) and a zero-initialized length-N gradient. Loop over each lag and add its weighted slice derivatives directly to that vector. For k≥0, with the a and b slices from 3.4, use w=(2/N)p[k+N−1], add w(1−b) to gradient entries k:k+L, and subtract w a from entries 0:L. For k<0, use d and L from 3.4, add w(1−b) to entries 0:L, and subtract w a from entries d:d+L. The k=0 updates combine to the required derivative. Implement a top-level smooth_value(h, τ, N) for line-search evaluations using q and the same stable formula, without computing a gradient.

3.6. Implement score_exact(h, N). Reject an incorrect shape or non-finite input with positive infinity. Otherwise compute np.correlate(h, 1.0−h, mode='full'), take its maximum over all 2N−1 entries, and multiply by 2.0/N. This direct expression is authoritative for initialization, candidate selection, fallback scoring, and final return. Do not report a smoothed score or a surrogate optimizer value.

3.7. Set the baseline to the supplied parent itself when it is finite, in [0,1], and already satisfies the sum constraint within floating-point tolerance; never mutate it. If a finite parent violates either constraint, use project_box_sum to make the baseline. If there is no usable finite parent, use the uniform vector. Initialize the global incumbent from this feasible baseline and its exact score before optimization. Keep the parent as the fallback when it is valid; all subsequent candidates must be new arrays so they cannot mutate a stored incumbent. For N=1, use the only feasible vector [0.5], compute its exact score, skip the search, and return it.

3.8. Build a deterministic start portfolio using the seeded generator, with every non-baseline start passed through project_box_sum. In this order use: the baseline; baseline plus 0.20 times an independent standard-normal vector; an independent uniform [0,1] vector; a smooth Fourier profile; the complement 1−baseline when a parent exists (otherwise 0.5 plus 0.4 times standard-normal noise); the uniform vector; baseline plus 0.08 times standard-normal noise; and baseline plus 0.40 times standard-normal noise. For the Fourier profile, use i=0,…,N−1 and R=min(6,floor((N−1)/2)); set z_i=0.5+Σ_{r=1}^R (0.12/r)[A_r sin(2πri/N)+B_r cos(2πri/N)], with independent standard-normal A_r and B_r, then project. For R=0 use the uniform vector. Consider every selected start itself as an exact-scored candidate.

3.9. Implement a top-level optimizer helper taking a feasible start, N, the current global incumbent vector and score, and the per-stage iteration limit; return the updated incumbent. Use the fixed temperature sequence [0.08, 0.02, 0.005, 0.001, 0.0002, 0.00004, 0.000008], in score units. For each temperature, initialize the local path at the prior stage’s selected point and initialize the stage-best point and score from it. At each iteration obtain φ and g from smooth_value_grad. Start a backtracking step size α=1.0. For at most 24 trials, project y=project_box_sum(h−αg,N), set d=y−h, and stop the stage’s line search if ||d||∞<1e−10. Compute g·d, smooth_value(y,τ,N), and score_exact(y,N). If y is feasible and its exact score is strictly smaller, update the global incumbent; also update the stage-best point if its exact score is strictly smaller than the current stage-best score. These exact-score updates apply even if the trial is not accepted by the smooth line search.

Accept a line-search step only when g·d<0 and φ_τ(y) ≤ φ_τ(h)+1e−4(g·d)+1e−14. On acceptance set h=y and increase the next trial’s starting step size to min(1.4α,10). On rejection halve α; stop backtracking if α<1e−8. If no step is accepted, end this temperature stage but continue to the next, lower temperature from the stage-best exact-score point. Also set the next stage’s starting point to the stage-best point after reaching the iteration limit. This preserves exact improvements found at rejected trials while allowing the smooth descent path to guide later proposals. Stop a stage early when an accepted displacement has infinity norm below 1e−8. Use no more than the per-stage iteration limit. Every optimizer exception or non-finite value must leave the incumbent unchanged and allow the next start to proceed.

3.10. In run, process the selected starts sequentially. Before each optimization, ensure its dimension, finiteness, and joint feasibility; exact-score it and update the incumbent only on a strict score decrease. Catch failures per start, retaining the feasible incumbent. Run the fixed temperature sequence for every selected start; do not fabricate a score or stop merely because a target score was hoped for. The exact incumbent is kept separately from each smooth optimization path, so a path that worsens the true maximum cannot displace a better candidate.

3.11. Before returning, check the incumbent shape, finiteness, bounds, and sum. If necessary, repair it once with project_box_sum. If repair or validation fails, replace it with the uniform vector. Recompute score_exact on the final vector after this check. If that score is not finite, return the uniform vector and its recomputed exact score. Return a one-dimensional float array, the Python float exact score, and int(N), in that order.

4. Search choices and useful variations
Correctness requirements are fixed: preserve a valid parent’s resolution, use all 2N−1 full linear-correlation lags, minimize the maximum, maintain both constraints jointly, and choose the returned candidate by the exact score. The default temperatures, start formulas, seed, projection, and line search are fully specified above. Use this deterministic adaptation for search effort: for N≤100 select all eight starts and use 60 iterations per temperature; for 101≤N≤200 select the first six starts and use 40 iterations per temperature; for 201≤N≤500 select the first four starts and use 20 iterations per temperature; for N>500 select the first three starts and use 8 iterations per temperature. With the stated start ordering, these reduced portfolios retain the baseline and varied starts. This keeps the default N=70 effort focused on the supplied construction while reducing work for larger parent dimensions.

A coder may use 6–10 starts when N≤100, 40–100 iterations per temperature for N≤100, or perturbation scales from 0.05 to 0.5, provided the baseline remains included and every proposal is projected and judged by score_exact. Fourier profiles may use 3–8 modes and amplitudes between approximately 0.08/r and 0.18/r. A lower final temperature down to 1e−6 is optional; use stable log-sum-exp and retain exact-score selection. These are search heuristics, not correctness changes or guarantees of a better bound. No resolution change is needed or permitted for the supplied parent.

5. Numerical robustness and memory use
Use float64 throughout. Stable log-sum-exp subtracts rmax before exponentiation; underflowed nonmaximal weights may be zero, while the maximum term ensures the normalization sum is at least one. Check all gradients, values, and proposals for finiteness. A non-finite proposal is discarded or repaired to the uniform feasible vector. The bounded step-size backtracking prevents blindly accepting a smooth-objective increase; if it cannot find a step, move on to the next temperature while keeping the best exact candidate. If a start or stage fails, preserve the incumbent and continue. If no improvement is found, the valid baseline remains available.

The lag values, softmax weights, gradient, h, and correlation output require O(N) memory. Do not construct a dense Hessian, an M-by-N lag-Jacobian matrix, or a pairwise tensor. Each full lag evaluation is O(N²) arithmetic across all lags; the supplied N=70 requires only 139 lags and is small. The reduced start and iteration schedule limits work if a larger parent is supplied. Run sequentially on the allowed single CPU. Projection bisection is O(80N), and the final score is calculated directly with the finite linear correlation. These methods provide no certificate of global optimality.

6. Runtime safeguards and return contract
The generated program must perform all input parsing, feasibility repair, optimization, candidate checks, exact scoring, failure handling, and fallback selection inside run and its top-level helpers. Check the parent’s shape and finite values before using its entries; preserve its valid dimension and never mutate it. Check each candidate’s expected shape and finiteness, ensure 0≤h_i≤1 and |sum(h)−N/2|≤1e−10·max(1,N), and repair with the capped-simplex projection when needed. Keep a feasible incumbent at all times. A valid parent is the initial fallback; otherwise the uniform vector is the guaranteed fallback.

For every comparison and for the final c5_bound, compute max(np.correlate(h, 1.0−h, mode='full'))*(2.0/N) from the candidate itself. The pre-imported evaluator is not a substitute for implementing this expression. Return exactly (h_values, c5_bound, n_points), with finite h_values in [0,1], the required sum to floating-point precision, c5_bound equal to the recomputed exact score, and n_points equal to the chosen runtime dimension. If nothing improves, return the valid baseline rather than claiming the target or reporting a surrogate value.
